emergency.notes: Mountain rescue: 140 (Alpine rescue). ÖAMTC road assistance: 120. All emergency operators speak German and English.

travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise normal precautions in Austria. Be aware of the potential for terrorism. Austria remains a stable and safe destination for tourists.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Most visits to Austria are trouble-free. There is a threat from terrorism. Check the avalanche forecast if skiing or hiking in alpine areas.

healthcare.costForTourists: EU citizens with EHIC receive care at Austrian public rates. Non-EU tourists pay full price. GP visit ~€50-100. Emergency room ~€200-500. Hospital stay €300-1,000+/night. Public hospitals are excellent.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (Apotheke) on every main street. After-hours emergency pharmacies operate on a rotating basis — a list is posted on each pharmacy door. Many pharmacists speak English.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Austria's public hospital system is excellent. Vienna General Hospital (AKH Wien) is one of the largest hospitals in the world. University hospitals in major cities have English-speaking staff.
vaccinationsRecommended: Tick-borne Encephalitis (TBE) if hiking in rural/forest areas, especially May-September
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance strongly recommended for non-EU visitors. EU citizens should carry their EHIC card. Consider ski/mountain rescue insurance if doing Alpine activities — rescue operations are very expensive.

controlledSubstances.note: Carry original prescription and a doctor's letter in German or English. For longer stays, obtain a Schengen certificate for narcotic medications.
Require original prescription. Maximum 1-month supply. A Schengen certificate is recommended for travel across multiple EU countries.
Controlled psychotropic substance. Carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Max 1-month supply.

medications.generalAdvice: Austria follows EU/Schengen regulations for controlled substances. EU prescriptions are generally accepted. Non-EU travelers should carry original packaging, a prescription, and a doctor's letter. For narcotics, a Schengen certificate valid for all countries visited is recommended.

scams.name: Concert / show ticket touts
scams.description: Men in Mozart costume near the Staatsoper and Hofburg sell tickets for classical concerts at inflated prices. The concerts themselves exist but are often mediocre tourist productions, not the prestigious venues implied.
scams.avoidance: Buy concert tickets directly from the Wiener Philharmoniker, Staatsoper, or Wien.info. If attending a period-costume show, research it online first.

scams.name: Ski resort equipment damage scam
scams.description: Rental shops claim pre-existing damage to skis or boots was caused by you and demand payment. Deposits can be held unfairly.
scams.avoidance: Photograph all rented equipment before use. Note any pre-existing damage in writing with the rental shop before leaving.

scams.name: Vienna Prater fake fortune tellers
scams.description: At the Prater amusement park, fortune tellers or charity collectors approach tourists with 'free readings' that end with aggressive donation demands.
scams.avoidance: Politely decline all unsolicited services. Only engage with official park attractions.

connectivity.simOptions: SIM cards from A1, Magenta (T-Mobile), or Drei at airports and shops. EU roaming rules apply for EU SIMs — no extra charge. Tourist SIM ~€10-20 for 10-30GB. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi widely available in hotels, cafes, restaurants, train stations (Wien Hauptbahnhof), and many public areas. Vienna has free public WiFi in many districts.
connectivity.bestOption: EU SIM travelers can use their home SIM under EU roaming rules. Others: Drei (3) Austria offers good value prepaid data. eSIM from Airalo for convenience.

cultural.tipping: Round up the bill or add 5-10% in restaurants. Say the amount you want to pay when handing over cash (e.g., 'Stimmt so' means keep the change). Tipping is appreciated but not mandatory.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual is standard. Vienna is a formal city — dress up for opera, fine dining, and churches. Cover shoulders and knees in churches.
cultural.greetings: Handshake is standard. Close friends greet with cheek kisses. Use formal titles (Herr/Frau + last name) until invited to use first names. Austrians value formality and punctuality.
taboos: Assuming all Austrians speak like Germans — there is regional pride
Being late to appointments or dinners
Overly casual behavior in formal settings (operas, museums)
Jaywalking — Austrians wait for pedestrian signals
cultural.haggling: Not practiced. Prices are fixed. Only at antique markets or private sales is negotiation sometimes possible.

safety.lgbtSafety: Very LGBTQ+ friendly. Same-sex registered partnerships and marriage are legal. Vienna has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Vienna Pride (Regenbogenparade) is one of Europe's major events.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Very safe. Austria consistently ranks among the safest European countries for women. Normal urban precautions apply at night.
safety.notes: Austria is one of the safest countries in Europe. The main risks for tourists are petty theft in crowded tourist areas and avalanche danger for Alpine activities. Vienna pickpocketing occurs on the U-Bahn and at major attractions.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK citizens: 90 days in any 180-day period. EU citizens: unlimited.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: December-March for skiing. April-June and September-October for mild temperatures and fewer crowds. July-August is peak summer (Vienna can be hot). Christmas markets (November-December) are iconic.

hospitals.name: Vienna General Hospital (AKH Wien)
hospitals.notes: One of the largest hospitals in the world. Full international department with English-speaking staff.

hospitals.name: LKH Innsbruck (University Hospital)
hospitals.notes: Main hospital for Tyrolean Alps region. Handles mountain rescue cases.

immediate: If caught in an avalanche, try to swim to the surface using breast-stroke motion
As snow slows, create breathing space in front of your mouth with your hands before it sets
Try to get an arm or hand toward the surface to help rescuers locate you
Stay calm and breathe slowly to conserve oxygen
Spit to determine which direction is down — snow settles upward
after: If someone is buried, mark the last-seen point and begin searching downslope
Use avalanche beacon (RECCO) to assist rescuers
Follow Austrian Alpine Club guidance for safe zones

immediate: Move to higher ground immediately if near a river or low-lying area
Do not drive through flooded roads
Turn off electricity at the mains if water enters your home
Follow instructions from local emergency services (Feuerwehr)
after: Do not return to flooded buildings until cleared by authorities
